clinicalPearls: An inducible urticaria in which itchy weals develop on skin exposed to cold, most typically as it rewarms after contact with cold air, water or objects
The ice-cube test is the key bedside investigation: an ice cube (usually in a thin bag to avoid wetting) is applied to the forearm and a weal appears on rewarming in a positive result
Most cases are acquired and idiopathic, arising in adolescents and young adults, and are usually self-limiting over a few years
The greatest danger is a systemic reaction from extensive cold exposure, particularly swimming in cold water, which can cause hypotension, collapse and even drowning
Angioedema of the lips can follow cold food or drink, and oropharyngeal swelling is a recognised hazard
Rare familial and secondary forms exist, the latter occasionally linked to cryoglobulins or infection, so atypical cases merit further evaluation

Management combines strict avoidance of sudden cold exposure with non-sedating antihistamines, with omalizumab reserved for resistant disease and adrenaline provision for those at risk of systemic reactions
reference.pathophysiology: Cold urticaria results from cold-triggered activation and degranulation of cutaneous mast cells, releasing histamine and other mediators that produce weals and, when exposure is extensive, systemic effects. In many patients the reaction is thought to involve cold-dependent autoantigens or IgE-mediated mechanisms, while secondary forms may relate to cryoglobulins or other cold-precipitable proteins associated with infection or systemic disease. Because the response scales with the area and duration of cold exposure, large surface-area cooling such as swimming can precipitate life-threatening mediator release.
additionalDifferentials: Cholinergic urticaria triggered in cold environments
additionalInvestigations: Ice-cube (cold-contact) provocation test to confirm the diagnosis and gauge threshold
History clarifying the rewarming pattern and any systemic symptoms with extensive exposure
Cryoglobulins and cold agglutinins in atypical or secondary cases
Full blood count and inflammatory markers where an underlying disorder is suspected
Screening for associated infection where clinically indicated
Assessment of systemic reaction risk to guide adrenaline provision
redFlags: History of faintness, wheeze or collapse with widespread cold exposure such as swimming
Oropharyngeal angioedema after cold food or drink
Atypical features suggesting cryoglobulinaemia or another systemic disorder
Onset in infancy or a family history suggesting a hereditary autoinflammatory syndrome
reference.prognosis: Acquired idiopathic cold urticaria commonly remits spontaneously within a few years and is well controlled with avoidance and antihistamines, but it carries a real risk of serious systemic reactions during large-area cold exposure, which patients must be counselled about; secondary forms follow the course of the underlying disorder.
pitfalls: Failing to warn patients against swimming in cold water because of the risk of systemic collapse and drowning
Omitting the simple ice-cube test that readily confirms the diagnosis
Not screening for cryoglobulins or infection in atypical or secondary presentations
Overlooking the need for an adrenaline auto-injector in those at risk of anaphylaxis
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on chronic urticaria
